content: Antibiotic treatments administered for one to three days can effectively shorten the duration of cholera and alleviate the severity of its symptoms. However, individuals can recover from cholera even without antibiotics, provided that adequate hydration and electrolyte balance are maintained throughout the course of the illness. Doxycycline is commonly used as the first-line antibiotic for cholera treatment. However, certain strains of Vibrio cholerae have demonstrated resistance to this medication. A single dose of 300 mg doxycycline or tetracycline at a dosage of 12.5 mg/kg administered four times daily for three days is often recommended. Other antibiotics that have been proven effective include cotrimoxazole, erythromycin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol, and furazolidone. Fluoroquinolones, such as norfloxacin, may also be utilized, although resistance to these agents has been reported in some cases. For young children, erythromycin is recommended at a dosage of 12.5 mg/kg administered four times daily for three days. For children under six months of age, zinc supplementation at a dose of 10 mg daily for 10 days is advised. For children aged six months to five years, zinc supplementation at a dose of 20 mg daily for 10 days is recommended. In many regions worldwide, antibiotic resistance is becoming increasingly prevalent. Testing for antibiotic resistance during cholera outbreaks can provide valuable information to guide the selection of appropriate treatment options. For instance, in Bangladesh, most cholera cases are resistant to tetracycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and erythromycin. Rapid diagnostic assays are available to identify cases of multidrug-resistant cholera, which can aid in timely and effective management. New-generation antimicrobials have been discovered and have shown efficacy against cholera in in vitro studies, offering potential alternatives for treatment in the face of rising antibiotic resistance.
